In *Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know* [[1]](#ref-1) (arXiv preprint, November 2022), [Saurav Kadavath](https://www.linkedin.com/in/saurav-kadavath/), [Jared Kaplan](https://sites.krieger.jhu.edu/jared-kaplan/), and co-authors at [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) ask whether a language model can judge the correctness of its own outputs and predict which questions it will get right.

> We study whether language models can evaluate the validity of their own claims and predict which questions they will be able to answer correctly. We first show that **larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions when they are provided in the right format**. Thus we can approach self-evaluation on open-ended sampling tasks by asking models to first propose answers, and then to evaluate the probability **"P(True)"** that their answers are correct. We find encouraging performance, calibration, and scaling for P(True) on a diverse array of tasks. **Performance at self-evaluation further improves when we allow models to consider many of their own samples before predicting the validity of one specific possibility.** Next, we investigate whether models can be trained to predict **"P(IK)", the probability that "I know" the answer to a question, without reference to any particular proposed answer**. **Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks, though they struggle with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks.** The predicted P(IK) probabilities also increase appropriately in the presence of relevant source materials in the context, and in the presence of hints towards the solution of mathematical word problems. We hope these observations lay the groundwork for training more honest models, and for investigating how honesty generalizes to cases where models are trained on objectives other than the imitation of human writing.

## Method

The paper runs three related studies on a family of Anthropic language models ranging up to 52B parameters. The first measures calibration on multiple-choice and true/false questions across BIG-Bench, MMLU, [TruthfulQA](/posts/20230226-truthfulqa-llm-truthfulness/), LogiQA, and QuALITY, varying format (visible letter options vs. none-of-the-above) and prompt regime (zero-shot vs. few-shot). The second introduces a self-evaluation procedure: the model samples an answer to an open-ended question, then is prompted to assign $P(\text{True})$ to its own sample, optionally after being shown several additional T=1 samples as context. The third trains a separate value head on top of the base model to predict $P(\text{IK})$ ("the probability I know the answer") on TriviaQA, Arithmetic, Python function synthesis, Lambada, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval, and tests how this head generalizes to held-out distributions, to the presence of source materials, and to math-problem hints.

## Results

The headline findings break down by experiment:

- **Lettered multiple choice, 5-shot.** Expected calibration error drops steadily with model scale on BIG-Bench and MMLU; the 52B model is well-calibrated on both (Figure 4).
- **"None of the above" breaks calibration, and the reason is revealing.** On MMLU the paper replaces *only* option (D) with the string "none of the above" (options A/B/C are untouched; total number of options unchanged). Accuracy falls sharply and the (D)-specific calibration curve collapses, with the model strongly biased against ever choosing "none of the above"; 5-shot and 20-shot prompting don't fix it. The mechanism: when all four options are concrete, the model's task is *relative*, ranking which of these strings is best-supported among the listed set. When one option is abstract, it requires an *independent* judgment: is any of the listed answers actually correct, or is the true answer missing? The paper's motivation for the ablation is that this exposes what lettered-MC calibration does *not* test on its own, a gap Figure 8's True/False setup then partially closes.
- **True/False restores it by forcing independent judgment per option.** Rephrasing the same multiple-choice items as standalone "Is X the correct answer to Q? (True/False)" items recovers calibration: the 52B model is well-calibrated except at the tails (Figure 8). The difference from "none of the above" is that True/False forces the model to evaluate each option in isolation without needing to detect that *all* listed options are wrong. That is the evidence for the paper's claim that models can judge options on absolute merit when asked one at a time.
- **RLHF policies need a temperature fix.** They look miscalibrated out of the box but a single temperature rescaling recovers calibration on the same benchmarks.
- **$P(\text{True})$ self-evaluation works at 52B.** Across TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval, the 52B model's self-assigned $P(\text{True})$ cleanly separates its correct from incorrect samples (left panel of Figure 1, the cover). Showing the model multiple T=1 samples before asking it to rate one improves both AUROC and calibration.
- **Trained $P(\text{IK})$ heads partially generalize.** They transfer across the six training tasks but are poorly calibrated on out-of-distribution tasks. They do respond appropriately, raising probability, when relevant source materials or correct hints are added to the context.

## My Notes

- **The $P(\text{IK})$ head probes self-knowledge more directly than the $P(\text{True})$ prompt does, and that distinction has held up in later work.** $P(\text{True})$ is prompt-only (no training): the model is shown its own sampled answer and asked to rate it, so the work it does is *evaluation* of content already on the page. $P(\text{IK})$ is a *trained* value head on top of the base model, supervised on per-question correctness labels, which asks the model to forecast its own future sampling behavior from the question alone. The training distinction is what makes $P(\text{IK})$ a genuine self-knowledge probe rather than an answer grader. Later work on eliciting latent knowledge and on probing hidden-state representations of truthfulness, including Burns et al.'s *Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision* [[2]](#ref-2), has mostly kept this split. The 2023–2024 hallucination literature still finds that sequence-level uncertainty signals beat token-logit entropy for open-ended tasks [[3]](#ref-3).
- **Format-dependent calibration is the caveat the field underweights.** The paper is often cited for "large models are calibrated," but the caveat is heavy: lettered multiple choice works, none-of-the-above breaks it, RLHF policies need a temperature fix (§4 of the paper), and $P(\text{IK})$ is poorly calibrated out of distribution. Any production deployment that reads raw softmax probabilities from a post-RLHF model should re-calibrate per domain rather than trust the model's raw outputs, because the format in which the question is asked matters as much as model scale does.
- **"Showing the model its own samples" connects to self-consistency and foreshadows SelfReflect's only positive result.** The improvement from giving the model several T=1 samples before asking it to rate one is the same underlying effect Wang et al. [[4]](#ref-4) document for majority-vote decoding, applied here to self-evaluation. Three years later the [SelfReflect](/posts/20260430-selfreflect-internal-distribution/) paper [[5]](#ref-5) finds the same mechanism is the *only* thing that lets modern LLMs describe their own answer distribution faithfully: across 20 models, prompting, chain-of-thought, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO) all fail, while sampling $N$ outputs and summarizing those works. Kadavath's 52B result and SelfReflect's negative sweep are the same observation at different stringency: models can evaluate content already on the page but cannot introspect their own distribution without the samples in context. The 2022 paper's open question (whether the sampling gain comes from better mode separation or from using the samples as a rough frequency estimate) is largely resolved by SelfReflect's decomposition: the samples *are* the introspection.
- **Scale mattered a lot in 2022, and the floor has moved. Format-dependence has not.** Every headline calibration result held at 52B and degraded sharply below ~10B at the time of writing. Three years later, 7–9B open models (Llama-3, Mistral, Gemma-2, Phi) have narrowed that gap on lettered-MC accuracy after instruction tuning, though I'm not aware of a head-to-head that directly replicates the 2022 BIG-Bench ECE bar at that scale. The follow-up calibration literature (semantic entropy [[6]](#ref-6), verbalized confidence on RLHF'd models [[7]](#ref-7)) shows sampling- and elicitation-based uncertainty signals work across the 7–70B range. What has not changed is the format-dependence half of the result: even frontier models still underuse "none of the above" and still lose calibration on open-ended generation without a sampling detour, per SelfReflect's 2026 sweep [[5]](#ref-5). Scale bought better calibration on favorable prompt formats. The absolute-correctness gap the none-of-the-above ablation exposed is still open.
